summary: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation, sedating H1-antihistamine of the ethanolamine class with marked anticholinergic, antiemetic and central sedative activity. It is used for symptomatic relief of allergic conditions (urticaria, allergic rhinitis, allergic reactions), as a short-term nighttime sleep aid, for motion sickness and for the management of drug-induced extrapyramidal/parkinsonian symptoms; parenterally it is also an adjunct in anaphylaxis. Because it readily crosses the blood-brain barrier it commonly causes drowsiness, and its anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision, confusion) are particularly problematic in older adults, in whom it is generally best avoided. Overdose can cause anticholinergic toxidrome, seizures, wide-complex arrhythmias and death.
indications: Symptomatic relief of allergic conditions: urticaria, angioedema, allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis and pruritus
Adjunctive therapy in anaphylaxis and other severe allergic reactions (parenteral)
Short-term relief of occasional sleeplessness (nighttime sleep aid)
Prevention and treatment of motion sickness
Treatment of drug-induced extrapyramidal reactions and parkinsonism (including acute dystonia)
Antitussive and cough/cold symptom relief (in combination OTC products)

moa: Diphenhydramine competitively and reversibly antagonizes histamine at peripheral and central H1 receptors, blocking histamine-mediated vascular permeability, smooth-muscle contraction, pruritus and nasal/conjunctival symptoms. It crosses the blood-brain barrier to produce central sedation and has antiemetic and antivertigo effects via central H1 and muscarinic blockade. Its substantial anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) activity accounts for both therapeutic effects (e.g. in drug-induced parkinsonism) and adverse effects such as dry mouth, urinary retention and confusion.

Use as a local anesthetic (topical) over large or raw/blistered areas due to systemic absorption risk

preg: Diphenhydramine has a long history of human use and is generally considered acceptable in pregnancy when needed; epidemiologic data have not shown a clear increase in major malformations. For OTC use, advise pregnant patients to ask a health professional before use, and use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.
lact: Diphenhydramine is excreted in small amounts in breast milk. First-generation antihistamines may cause sedation or irritability in the breastfed infant and may reduce milk supply. Use with caution; occasional low doses are generally tolerated, but avoid regular high-dose use during lactation.
renal: In significant renal impairment, clearance is reduced; lengthen the dosing interval and use the lowest effective dose to limit accumulation and sedation.
hepatic: Diphenhydramine is extensively metabolized in the liver. In hepatic impairment, reduced clearance can increase and prolong sedation and anticholinergic effects; use with caution and consider lower or less frequent dosing.

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors - prolong and intensify anticholinergic effects; avoid
Alcohol and CNS depressants (opioids, benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics) - additive CNS depression and respiratory depression
moderate: Other anticholinergic drugs (tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiparkinson agents, antispasmodics) - additive anticholinergic toxicity
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors - may increase diphenhydramine levels; diphenhydramine itself inhibits CYP2D6 and can raise levels of CYP2D6 substrates (e.g. metoprolol)
minor: Drugs requiring intact skin testing - antihistamines suppress wheal/flare responses (stop several days before allergy testing)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food can reduce gastric upset.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol because of additive sedation and impaired psychomotor performance.
interactions.diagnostics: Suppresses cutaneous histamine responses - discontinue at least 72 hours before skin allergy testing to avoid false-negative results.

missed: If you take diphenhydramine on a schedule and miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume your normal schedule. Do not double up. For occasional use (allergy symptoms, sleep), simply take a dose only when needed within the labeled limits.
overdose: Overdose produces an anticholinergic toxidrome: dilated pupils, flushed dry skin, fever, urinary retention, agitation or delirium, hallucinations and, in severe cases, seizures, wide-complex (sodium-channel-blocking) arrhythmias, hypotension, coma and death; children are especially sensitive. There is no specific routine antidote; treat with supportive care, activated charcoal if early, benzodiazepines for seizures/agitation, sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening, and physostigmine only in selected severe pure anticholinergic toxicity. Get emergency help or contact a poison control center.
